page_summary:
Ted Barton returns as an adult to his childhood town of Millgate, Virginia, only to find it utterly unrecognizable -- buildings, streets, and even the town's remembered history have been altered, and official records insist he died there as a child years earlier. Barton discovers that the town is the battleground of an ongoing cosmic conflict between figures drawn from Zoroastrian mythology: Ahriman, the destructive spirit, has seized control of Millgate and rewritten its reality and history according to his own design, while Ormazd, the creative spirit, works covertly through a young girl named Mary to restore the town's true, original form. Barton becomes caught between these mythic forces, his own erased identity and memory serving as both casualty and battleground of the struggle, with the novel's resolution turning on whether the original, 'true' Millgate -- and Barton's own genuine remembered life -- can be restored against Ahriman's fabricated overlay.

**Why it matters.** The Cosmic Puppets, expanded from Dick's 1953 novella A Glass of Darkness, is one of his earliest sustained engagements with reality-alteration as a literalized battleground between opposing cosmic or theological forces, directly anticipating the reality-instability and gnostic dualism that would become central to his mature fiction and, eventually, the Exegesis. Its explicit use of Zoroastrian mythology (Ahriman and Ormazd) as active, reality-shaping combatants rather than abstract religious symbols marks an early instance of Dick's recurring interest in treating world religious and mythological traditions as literal metaphysical mechanisms rather than mere belief systems.

*The restoration of Millgate's true form resolves the immediate conflict but leaves the larger cosmic struggle between Ahriman and Ormazd implicitly ongoing, consistent with Dick's general reluctance to grant any single victory final, permanent status.*
